changes.modelAnswer: A growing long bone consists of a shaft or diaphysis, two ends or epiphyses, and between them the metaphysis, which is the part of the diaphysis adjoining the epiphyseal plate. The epiphyseal (growth) plate is a disc of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and the metaphysis; it is a primary cartilaginous joint and is responsible for growth of the bone in length, disappearing when growth ceases. The shaft is a tube of compact bone enclosing a medullary cavity that contains marrow whose red/yellow composition changes with age, with red marrow predominant in young children and is lined by endosteum, while the epiphyses are made of spongy bone containing red marrow and are covered at the joint by articular hyaline cartilage. The whole bone except the articular surfaces is covered by periosteum, which is responsible for growth in diameter and for the nutrition and repair of the bone. The bone is supplied by a nutrient artery to the shaft, together with periosteal, metaphyseal and epiphyseal vessels.

changes.modelAnswer: Joint stability depends on three groups of factors. The first is bony, that is the shape and mutual fit of the articular surfaces, which is the dominant factor in the hip. The second is ligamentous, the capsule and the intrinsic and extrinsic ligaments that check excessive movement. The third and most important in most joints is muscular, the tone of the muscles crossing the joint, which is why the shoulder, with shallow surfaces and lax ligaments, depends on the rotator cuff. Atmospheric pressure and the vacuum effect of the closed joint, and accessory structures such as labra and menisci, give additional stability. Ligaments are strong, mostly resistant to stretch, although some ligaments contain abundant elastic fibers bands of dense fibrous tissue that permit normal movement but resist abnormal movement; they are poorly vascular, so a torn ligament (sprain) heals slowly, and they carry proprioceptive nerve endings that reflexly protect the joint.
changes.explanation: Joint stability depends on articular shape, ligaments and muscle tone. Most ligaments contain dense collagen and resist excessive movement, but some, such as vertebral elastic ligaments, can stretch and recoil. Healing and vascularity vary by ligament.

changes.modelAnswer: Muscles with parallel fibres run in the long axis of the muscle and give a wide range of movement but less power; they may be strap-like as the sartorius, fusiform as the biceps brachii, quadrilateral as the pronator quadratus. Convergent muscles have fan-shaped fibres, as in the temporalis. Pennate muscles have fibres set obliquely on a tendon like a feather and are more powerful but shorter in range: unipennate, with the tendon on one side, as the flexor pollicis longus; bipennate, with the tendon in the middle, as the dorsal interossei and rectus femoris; multipennate, with several tendinous septa, as the deltoid; and circumpennate, with the fibres converging on a central tendon from all round, as the tibialis anterior. Other muscles are cruciate, with crossing fibres, as the sternocleidomastoid, or spiral, as the trapezius and latissimus dorsi. Sphincteric (circular) muscles such as the orbicularis oris surround an orifice and close it.
changes.keyConcept: Shapes: parallel (sartorius), unipennate (FPL), bipennate (dorsal interosseous), multipennate (deltoid), circumpennate (tibialis anterior), cruciate (SCM), spiral (trapezius).

changes.modelAnswer: There are 3 1 pairs of spinal nerves, each formed within the intervertebral foramen by the union of a dorsal and a ventral root. The dorsal root is purely sensory and bears the dorsal root ganglion, which contains the cell bodies of the unipolar sensory neurons; the ventral root is purely motor and carries the axons of the anterior horn cells, together with preganglionic sympathetic fibres in the T1-L2 segments and preganglionic parasympathetic fibres in the S2, S3 and S4 segments. The resulting spinal nerve trunk is therefore mixed, and it is extremely short, dividing at once into a small dorsal ramus, which supplies the skin and the true muscles of the back, and a large ventral ramus, which supplies the rest of the trunk and the limbs and forms the nerve plexuses. The ventral ramus is connected to the sympathetic chain by a white ramus communicans (only T1-L2, carrying myelinated preganglionic fibres) and by a grey ramus communicans (present at every level, carrying non-myelinated postganglionic fibres).

changes.keyConcept: Spermatogenesis (60-6 4 days) = proliferation, growth, maturation (meiosis) and transformation (spermiogenesis).
changes.modelAnswer: Spermatogenesis is the sequence of events by which the primitive germ cells of the seminiferous tubules, the spermatogonia, are converted into mature spermatozoa; it begins at puberty and continues throughout life, and it takes about 60-6 4 days. It passes through four phases. In the proliferation phase the spermatogonia multiply repeatedly by mitosis. In the growth phase one daughter cell enlarges to become the primary spermatocyte, the largest cell of the series. In the maturation phase the primary spermatocyte undergoes the first meiotic (reduction) division to give two haploid secondary spermatocytes, each of which divides again in the second meiotic division to give two spermatids, so that four spermatids arise from each primary spermatocyte. In the transformation phase (spermiogenesis) each spermatid is remodelled, without further division, into a spermatozoon.
